analytic.title: Performance Evaluations and Estimations of Workload of On-Demand Updates in Soft Real-Time Systems *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Data being used in real-time systems must be up-to-date to produce correct results. The use of outdated data can have catastrophic consequences since calculated control signals are based on stale data. Two distinct methods to update data exist: (i) dedicated tasks (DT) update data items, and (ii) on-demand (OD) updating being a conditioned part of the execution flow of tasks. On-demand updating has not been studied in terms of CPU utilization analysis for real-time systems. This paper studies on-demand updating in terms of (i) imposed workload and compares the workload to Deferrable Scheduling (DS), and (ii) analytical formula for estimating workload to be used in CPU utilization based schedulability tests. It is found that on-demand updating uses less workload for updates compared to DS, which suggests on-demand updating should be used for resource constrained systems. However, using on-demand updating makes the execution times of updates unpredictable, which currently gives two possibilities (i) be pessimistic and assume all updates always execute or (ii) be less pessimistic but estimate the times between executions of updates. This paper devises a formula for such estimates and compares their result to approach (i). Evaluations show the formula can be useful for soft real-time systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many applications, but not limited to only real-time systems, need up-to-date data items. Data reflects values of entities where physical limitations, e.g., that the speed change of piston movement in an engine is bounded, indicate how long time data values can be considered to be up-to-date. Thus, a data item d i can be associated with an absolute validity interval, AV I(d i ), stating how old values are allowed to be [12]. Now, a straightforward method to ensure a data item is up-to-date is to use a periodic dedicated task updating the data item and set the task's period time to half its absolute validity interval. Using this approach, the maximum distance between two updates is AV I(d i ) since the update can occur at the beginning of one period and at the end of the following period [12,15]. This method is denoted Half-Half (HH). There are two important questions now: (Q1) Is the system, including dedicated tasks performing updates, schedulable? (Q2) What is the imposed workload of the updates?

There is a correlation between the two questions above. If the workload of updates is high it might render the system unschedulable. In the context of a hard real-time system, the first question is the most important. The second question is of interest for soft real-time systems or generalpurpose systems since an under/overloaded classification is sometimes allowed to be wrong because deadline misses can be tolerated. The workload approach might be both computationally cheaper to calculate compared to checking schedulability and less pessimistic. One way to calculate workload is to use an estimation technique. If estimation techniques are fast and accurate enough they could be used in on-line CPU utilization based schedulability tests. This paper investigates possible estimation techniques and their accuracy.

Performance evaluations in this paper show that ondemand updating imposes less workload compared to Deferrable Scheduling (DS), which is the, to date, algorithm reducing workload imposed by dedicated updating tasks the most [13,14]. This finding suggests that on-demand updating of data items is a strategy suitable for resource constrained embedded systems. However, on-demand updating in periodic tasks makes the updating activity event-based, because when updates occur depends on (i) the period times and phasings of tasks issuing on-demand updating and (ii) the condition that must be fulfilled in order to execute the update. This affects the possibility to answer questions Q1 and Q2. This paper presents methods-in the context of ondemand updates in periodic tasks-to give fast estimates of Q2. The contributions are:

• A formula that answers Q2 by estimating the mean interarrival times of executions of an on-demand update that uses AVI to measure data freshness. The formula calculates the estimation by using a probability density function of distances between arrival times of a set of tasks. The formula looks as follows and it is presented in Section 4:
div.formula: M IT (y, P) = E[P] -Q(y, P) y 0 q(x, P)xdx 1 -Q(y, P)
div.p: The probability density function (pdf), q(y, P), describes the distances between arrival times of a set P of tasks. The pdf, in the case of periodic tasks, can be described by a result of Cox and Smith [4].

• Performance evaluations show that the estimation given above is fast and give accurate values. Further, the evaluations show that the workload imposed by updates is lower when using on-demand updates compared to using dedicated tasks scheduled by Deferrable Scheduling.

The outline of this paper is as follows: Section 2 gives related work. Section 3 presents the data and task model used in this paper and gives some background on schedulability tests. Section 4 gives an analytical formula for mean interarrival time of execution of on-demand updates. Section 5 presents evaluations of the accuracy of the derived formula. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper.

div.head: Related Work and Motivation
div.p: In the area of real-time systems, keeping data values upto-date has previously been studied. As discussed in the introduction, there are two ways to determine when to update a data item: either by a dedicated task (DT) executed often enough, or on-demand (OD). Also, two ways to measure data freshness have been devised, namely (i) time domain (TD), e.g., AVIs, and (ii) value domain (VD), e.g., similarity. Thus, there are four ways to configure a system with respect to updating data items: DT+TD, DT+VD, OD+TD, and OD+VD. We now describe previous research in the different configurations.

In the area of AVI and dedicated tasks (DT+TD), techniques have been derived that decrease CPU utilization needed by the dedicated tasks, but yet allowing for sufficient schedulability tests [13][14][15]. HH and DS are two examples of these techniques and DS is, to this date, the technique reducing workload imposed by updates the most [13,14]. As the techniques become more complicated in order to reduce CPU workload further, the analysis of schedulability and CPU workload also become more complicated. For instance, CPU workload using DS can only be estimated using the algorithm in Figure 1 [14]. The estimate's accuracy has not been stated, but in [14] the measured workload and the estimated workload are very close.

In the area of AVI and on-demand updating (OD+TD), Ahmed and Vrbsky constructed algorithms for soft realtime systems [2]. Arbitrary data relationships are supported, i.e., derived items can depend on values of other derived items. Data relationships are normally described in terms of base items representing entities of the environment and derived items that only depend on base items. Examples of work considering such data models are [9,14]. No schedulability analysis is given in [2] nor any estimates of how often updates execute, i.e., the system is not analyzable.

Kuo and Mok formalized the notion of similarity, which says that two values of a data item can be considered similar if and only if they differ not more than a predefined amount [10,11]. Thus, similarity measures the freshness of a data item in the value-domain. In the area of similarity and dedicated tasks (DT+VD), data validity bounds have been used to determine how long period times of tasks can be enlarged in order to reduce workload imposed by updates [8]. Thus, changes of values are translated into how long time a value can be considered up-to-date, which resembles AVIs, that is then used to enlarge the period times. Analyzability can be achieved by using RM or Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and a CPU utilization test since tasks are periodic.

In the area of similarity and on-demand updating (OD+VD), arbitrary data relationships are considered [5][6][7]. It has been shown using simulations and real-life proof-ofconcepts that this technique uses the CPU resource more efficient than periodic tasks using AVI, i.e., Half-Half, and Ahmed and Vrbsky's work. However, since on-demand updating and arbitrary graphs are used it is hard to analyze the system since it is impossible to know at which time a given data item will be updated because it depends on how other data items have changed. Thus, only estimates of workload of updates can be given.

In this paper we limit the data and task model to contain base items and derived items that are derived only from base items and tasks that use on-demand updating using AVIs. This is done in order to investigate whether there are any

• estimation techniques of workload when using ondemand updating. Further, it is of interest to investigate the accuracy and computational complexity of the estimation techniques to decide whether they are usable in on-line CPU utilization schedulability tests.

• performance differences between on-demand updating and DS, which is the, to this date, method that bests utilizes the CPU using dedicated tasks for updates. Note that it has previously been found that on-demand updating may perform better than other methods [1]. However, this is an old result and it does not consider estimation of performance.

It may be possible to relax the assumption that derived data items can only depend on base items by using results presented in this paper. It is our future work to study this. It may also be possible to extend the results of the estimation formula to on-demand updates using similarity.

div.head: Data and Task Model
div.p: As mentioned in Section 2 this paper focuses on studying base items and derived items that only can be derived from base items. The data items being used in the system consists thus of two sets. The tasks in the system are periodic and for each task its deadline equals its period time. Each task derives one derived item and uses the value, e.g., sets an actuator. The system uses on-demand updating and all tasks determine if a data item should be updated based on AVIs. The tasks look conceptually as in Figure 2. In Figure 2, cT() is a function that returns the current time of the system, lastUpdTime is an array holding the times the base items were last updated, and AVI is an array of the AVIs of the base items.

div.head: Workload and Schedulability Tests
div.p: For scheduling of periodic tasks, there exist the Rate Monotonic (RM) and the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithms that both have schedulability tests [3]. The CPU utilization based schedulability test works by calculating the CPU utilization of each individual task and then comparing the sum of utilizations to a bound that is scheduling algorithm specific. Thus,
div.formula: m i=1 C i P i ≤ Bound,(1)
div.p: where C i is the worst-case execution time of task i, P i is the period time of the same task, and Bound depends on the scheduling algorithm being used. The test in Equation (1) works if the deadline equals the period time and that each task is independent, i.e., no synchronization mechanism is used. When using on-demand updating we note that a part of C i constitutes the on-demand updating. Thus, Equation (1) can be rewritten as follows:
div.formula: n i=1 od 1 i wcet(b 1 ) + • • • + od m i wcet(b m ) + CW OD i P i = wcet(b 1 ) n i=1 od 1 i P i + + • • • + n i=1 CW OD i P i ≤ Bound,(2
div.p: ) where wcet(b 1 ) is the worst-case execution time of ondemand updating of b 1 , od 1 i = 1 if task i has an on-demand update of b 1 , otherwise od 1 i = 0, and CW OD i is the execution time without on-demand updating of task i. Hence, CW OD i is the worst-case execution time that is used when dedicated tasks are used. The mean interarrival time of a set of n periodic events is [4]:
div.formula: P i + • • • + n i=1 CW OD i P i = wcet(b i ) M IT (b 1 ) + • • • + wcet(b m ) M IT (b m ) + n i=1 CW OD i P i ≤ Bound.
div.p: (4) Equation ( 4) relates to Equation (1) in that the left hand side part of Equation ( 1) is equal to the left hand side of Equation ( 4), which is shown using equations ( 3) and (2). Equation ( 4) means that the mean interarrival times of ondemand updates contribute to the schedulability of the system. However, Equation ( 4) assumes the worst-case scenario where all on-demand updates are always executed.

div.head: Estimation of Mean Interarrival Times of On-Demand Updates
div.p: This section presents an analytical formula that answers the important question Q2: 'What is the imposed workload of the updates?' of a system adhering to the task model in Section 3.

Equation ( 4) describes the CPU utilization under the assumption that every on-demand update need to be executed. However, the if-statements in Figure 2 guard the on-demand updates so we know that an update is not needed during the following AV I(d i ) time units from the time the update wrote the value of the updated data item. Thus, we want to calculate the mean interarrival time of an on-demand update when we know its AVI and the interarrival times of the tasks that use the on-demand update. We have devised a formula that derives the mean interarrival times of the execution of on-demand updates. The formula uses a probability density function describing the distribution of distances between task arrival times of the tasks that use the on-demand update, because it is assumed the on-demand updates are at the start of the tasks:
div.formula: M IT (y, P) = M × E[P] -M × Q(y, P) y 0 q(x, P)xdx M -M × Q(y, P) ,(5)
div.p: where M will cancel but it denotes the number of distances used to derive the probability density function under study and P is the set of tasks having a particular ondemand update and thus yielding the probability density function. E[P] is the expected value of the pdf given the input P and E[P] can be calculated by Equation (3). Thus, M × E[P] gives the total sum of the distances. Q(y, P) is the cumulative density function and states the fraction of distances being less than y. Further, M × Q(y, P) is the number of distances less than y. The product M × Q(y, P) y 0 q(x)xdx is the sum of distances less than y. The denominator calculates the number of distances remaining if those less than y are removed. The number of distances M in Equation ( 5) cancels. Hence, Equation ( 5) calculates the mean of distances greater than y, which is an estimation of the expected mean interarrival time between executions of the on-demand update with AVI equal to y.

In order to use Equation ( 5) to remove pessimism in the schedulability test described by Equation (4), we must find a probability density function that describes the distances between arrivals of periodic tasks. Cox and Smith have developed such a probability density function. Thus, in Equation ( 5) the following substitutions can be done: q(y, P)

div.p: P k , and Q(y, P) = y 0 q(x, P)dx, where N is the number of periodic tasks in P using the on-demand update that we want to know the mean interarrival time of and P i is one of these tasks. The substitution yields M IT (AV I(b i ), P) (Equation ( 5)) to produce an estimate of the mean interarrival time of the execution of the on-demand update. M IT (AV I(b i ), P) can now substitute M IT (b i ) in Equation ( 4) to remove the pessimism of assuming every on-demand update always execute.

This can efficiently be achieved using Simpson's rule where a segment of the integral can be estimated using b a f (x)dx ≈ b-a 6 (f (a) + 4f ((a + b)/2) + f (b)). Thus, the computational complexity of Equation ( 5) is polynomial in the size of the value of y since the interval [0, y] (or the interval [0, z] if Equation ( 6) is used) is divided into a polynomial number of segments. To give an idea of the execution times of Equation (5) using q(y, P) and r(z, P), and the algorithm in Figure 3, which constructs a timeline of task arrivals and estimates M IT (y, P) from the timeline, the following performance evaluations have been performed. A task set of 5 periodic tasks with ondemand updates has been used. max in the algorithm in Figure 3 is set to 100000. Equation ( 5) and the algorithm are executed 1000 times for 78 simulations and the average execution time is derived. Simpson's rule is used and the interval is divided into 10 segments. The computer is a Mac mini 1.25GHz PowerPC with 512MB memory and the Java runtime system is Apple's Java 1.5 implementation. The average execution time of Equation ( 5) using q(y, P) is 0.72 ± 0.02 ms, using r(z, P) is 0.016 ± 0.0002 ms, and the algorithm in Figure 3 is 1.15 ± 0.04 ms. Hence, this indicates that Equation ( 5) is 71.9 times faster than the timeline approach. Depending on the CPU being used, the execution time of Equation (5) using q(y, P) or r(z) may be low enough to be usable in on-line CPU utilization tests.

The running time of the algorithm in Figure 3 is pseudopolynomial if a correct mean interarrival time should be achieved since max must be set to the hyper-period of tasks' period times [3]. However, max can be set to a value much larger than the period times of the tasks and give a mean interarrival time is close to the result if max were set to the hyper-period.

To summarize this section, we have proposed a formula that estimates the mean interarrival time of executions of on-demand updates. The formula uses probability density functions that describe distances between arrivals of tasks. div.head: Performance Evaluations
div.p: This section evaluates the performance of using ondemand updates or dedicated tasks as well as accuracy of the formula M IT (AV I(b i ), P) presented in Section 4.
The evaluations show that:

• In a setting where systems are overloaded according to the baseline, which is Equation (2), i.e., it is assumed every on-demand update is always executed, we note that as the AVI increases the fraction of systems being unschedulable decreases. This is an expected behavior since as the AVI increases the number of times on-demand updates need to execute decreases.
• Over a varied number of tasks and varied AVI of a data item the workload imposed by updates of ondemand updating is always less than that of Deferrable Scheduling.

The remainder of this section is outlined as follows. Section 5.1 presents the simulator setup, Section 5.2 presents evaluations of workload of updates, and Section 5.3 gives a test of the accuracy of estimations in a practical setting.

div.head: Simulator Setup
div.p: The simulations are performed in a discrete-event simulator written in Java. The simulated system consists of a set of base items and a set of tasks that calculate derived items. Each base item is used by a specified number of tasks. The period times of the tasks are randomly chosen from a uniform distribution. The execution times of the tasks consist of two parts (i) on-demand updates and (ii) the computation. The execution time of an on-demand update is 1 time unit if it executes, otherwise it is 0. The computation always executes and its execution time is randomly chosen at simulation start-up time.

div.head: Performance Evaluations of Workload
div.p: In the first setting, the system has one base item and the number of tasks and the AVI of the base item is varied. The AVI is determined by taking a fraction of the lowest period time in the system. The period times are integers and chosen randomly from U (50, 1000) and the execution times of the computations are set to 1. The scheduling algorithm used is RM. We are now interested in measuring the workload imposed by on-demand updates which is done by taking the worst-case execution time of the update divided by the mean interarrival time of its execution. The workload of the ondemand update is compared to the workload imposed if Deferrable Scheduling were used. In the case of one data item, DS sets a dedicated updating task's period time to the data item's AVI minus one (see Figure 1 for the pseudo-code of DS). Figure 4 shows the smallest observed ratio (workload imposed by DS)/(workload imposed by OD) for each AVI fraction. We make the following observations: • The number of tasks influences the ratio in that it decreases as the number of tasks increases. The reason is that the higher the number of tasks the more likely it is that a task starts to execute at AV I(b i ) time units since b i was last updated, which gives an imposed workload close to wcet(b i )/AV I(b i ).

• The ratio is high, above 2, for small number of tasks. This is expected as described above. If the number of tasks is low it is very likely that the time between updates is larger than AV I(b i ) since there is no task starting close to AV I(b i ) time units since the last update. With this reasoning OD can be arbitrarily better than DS.

• As the AVI increases the likelihood that a task starts to execute after AV I(b i ) time units increases even for a small number of tasks. Thus, the ratio decreases as the AVI increases even for a small number of tasks. This can be seen in the figure.

Figure 5 shows the workload when each task has 10 ondemand updates, i.e., there are 10 base items in the system in this setting. The same parameters are used as above. If a deadline is missed, then that system's parameters are chosen again and the system is re-simulated. As we can see, the general behavior is as observed in Figure 4. However, for some simulated systems and for low AVI fraction and low number of tasks the ratio is low, but always above 1. The reason is that the phasing of the execution of the ondemand updates is such that few of them can be skipped. We observed this behavior only on 12% of the 0.05 AVI fraction systems. This constitutes 0.6% of all the simulated systems.

In summary, we observe that OD imposes less workload than DS and that OD can be arbitrarily better than DS. There exist settings, many on-demand updates are used in tasks, that give high workload of updates. However, the workload is lower than DS, because the period times assigned by DS are lower than the AVIs (see line 6 in Figure 1) and using on-demand updating gives that the time between updates cannot be lower than the AVI.

div.head: Performance Evaluations of Estimations
div.p: In this experiment, we evaluate the accuracy of Equation ( 5) as used in the schedulability test described in Equation (7). Simulations are run that are overloaded according to Equation (2), which constitutes our baseline since there exists no other known, to our best knowledge, schedulability test for on-demand updating. The number of base items is varied. Five tasks read each base item. The AVI of each base item is set to a fraction of the shortest period time in the simulation. The period times are integers and derived from U (20, 2000). The execution time of each update is 1 time unit and the execution time of each tasks' computation is an integer and randomly chosen from U (1,15). Each setting of number of tasks and fraction of AVI is run 100 times with new period times and execution times each run. Each simulation run is started once the random values give a total utilization, according to Equation (2), that lies between 1 and 1.04, i.e., the system is lightly overloaded according to the baseline and the scheduling algorithm being used is EDF. The simulator runs for 500000 time units and checks if there were deadline misses.

Figure 6 shows the number of systems that the baseline classifies correctly as overloaded. Note that if the baseline were correct 100 systems would always be unschedulable. We note the following: (i) The pessimism in the baseline increases as the AVI increases. This is expected since the longer the AVI the less often on-demand updates need to execute. (ii) The pessimism also increases as the number of tasks increases. This is also an expected behavior since as the number of tasks increases the number of times ondemand updates is accounted for in the schedulability test increases.

Figure 7 shows the minimal number of correct classifications of systems as overloaded or underloaded. All AVI fractions for each number of tasks are considered. 'MIT' is using Equation (5) with q(y, P), 'Timeline' is an estimation based on drawing a timeline of task arrivals as described by the algorithm in Figure 3, and 'Fast MIT' is using Equation (5) with r(z, P). We see that in the worst observed cases, 'MIT' gives an accuracy of 91%, 'Baseline' of only 14%, 'Timeline' of 89%, and 'Fast MIT' of 60%. Figure 8 shows the mean number of correctly classified systems and it is 95% or above for 'MIT'. 'Fast MIT' has a mean accuracy above 80%, which could be acceptable for some systems. However, the running time of 'Fast MIT' is considerably shorter than 'MIT' and 'Timeline' as shown in Section 4. The mean classification accuracy of the baseline is 57%.

In this paper's evaluations all execution times and period times are integers and on-demand updates execute for one time unit if the condition is fulfilled, otherwise they execute for zero time units. Thus, on-demand updates are never preempted. Preemptions of the updates can happen in real-life applications and could be resolved with, e.g., Priority Ceiling Protocol or turning off interrupts. If execution times of updates are short, which they usually are in real-time embedded systems, we do not believe using, e.g., PCP, will affect the evaluated accuracy of Equation (7) since it has already several uncertainties affecting its accuracy, e.g., the pdf and jitter of tasks. Short blocking times might not add to tasks' jitter nor to the fact that tasks do not start at their arrival as the pdf assumes. However, we intend to investigate this as part of our future work.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Work
div.p: In this paper, we recognize that real-time and embedded system's performance of on-demand updating has not been well studied. The motivation of remedying this is that on-demand updating constitutes an intuitive way to implement updating of data instead of using dedicated tasks to perform updates. Further, our performance evaluations show that on-demand updating using absolute validity intervals (AVIs) use CPU resources significantly better than Deferrable Scheduling that is the, to this date, best known method to execute dedicated updating tasks. This better performance also motivates the need to further investigate analyzability and estimation techniques of on-demand updating.
This paper shows one new estimation technique of mean interarrival time of on-demand updates' execution. The estimate's properties are:

• Fast to execute. It takes 0.016 ms to estimate mean interarrival time for each data item (1.15 ms using the timeline approach, the speed increase is 71.9 times). This estimate's accuracy is 60% in its worst observed case and above 80% in the mean case, which may be usable for some systems. Using a probability density function that is more accurate, but takes longer time to create gives an accuracy of 91% in the worst case and above 95% in the mean case. The running time is instead 0.72 ms.
• Good accuracy in the case of one on-demand update in each task. As summarized above, the accuracy is above 91%. The baseline's mean performance is 57%.

• Good accuracy in the case of several on-demand updates in each task, but there can be situations where the phasing of tasks make fewer on-demand update skips possible than our proposed formula proposes. We observed 0.6% of systems in a simulation to be of this kind. We argue that the algorithm that calculates workload imposed by updates when using DS can be used as an upper bound of workload imposed by on-demand updates.

Hence, the presented results in this paper help increase the usability of on-demand updates in real-time and embedded systems. On-demand updates are shown to significantly reduce workload imposed by updates compared to other updating techniques. In addition, if on-demand updating is used in soft real-time systems then the presented analytical formula can be used in CPU utilization based schedulability tests.
Based on this paper, our future work is (i) to relax the assumption that derived data is only derived from base data and (ii) to extend the analytical formula for systems using similarity.
